content.text: The static keyword is a non-access modifier in Java. It allows variables, methods, blocks, and nested classes to belong to the class rather than any instance of the class.

rows: Shared by all instances of a class (i.e., class variables).
Can be called without creating an object. Only access static members.
Executed once when the class is loaded, regardless of object creation.
Used for importing static members directly (covered later).

items: Shared across all instances — one copy per class.
Accessible using the class name or an object reference.
Do not access instance (non-static) variables or methods directly.
Executed once, when the class is loaded (before the constructor or main method).

content.text: Scenario: balance is a common initial value for all accounts.

content.code:
Account.getBalance();      // Accessing static method
System.out.println(Account.balance);  // Accessing static variable

items: JVM calls main() without creating an instance of the class.

sections.heading: Why Static Methods Cannot Be Overridden

items: Static methods belong to the class, not instances.
Method overriding relies on dynamic (runtime) dispatch — this applies only to instance methods.
Static methods use compile-time binding, so the method call is resolved at compile time, not at runtime.

content.text: You can declare a static method with the same signature in the subclass — this is called method hiding, not overriding.
Even though p refers to a Child object, the method from Parent is called because static methods are resolved using the reference type, not the object type.

rows: One copy shared across all objects
Belongs to the class; cannot access non-static members
Runs once when the class is loaded
Static because JVM does not instantiate the class
